paragraphs: The paper studies how to solve learning problems with ℓ0 regularization using branch-and-bound algorithms. These algorithms search different regions of the feasible space and use pruning tests to rule out regions that do not contain solutions worth pursuing. The practical difficulty is that standard pruning tests require solving convex optimization problems. Repeating that work throughout a search can become a computational bottleneck.

The authors propose an alternative pruning procedure for a generic family of these regularized problems. Its distinguishing feature is that it can assess several regions simultaneously. It can also be inserted into standard branch-and-bound implementations with negligible computational overhead, making the contribution a change to how the search eliminates regions rather than a replacement for the whole solver.

Numerical simulations show that this strategy can reduce solving time by several orders of magnitude on typical machine-learning problems. The result supports more efficient pruning as a powerful way to accelerate these searches, with the stated gains applying to the tested problems and the framework’s supported family.
icml-2024-a-new-branch-and-bound-pruning.tldr: A pruning procedure that assesses multiple search regions together can substantially accelerate branch-and-bound for a family of ℓ0-regularized learning problems.

paragraphs: Diffusion models typically generate an image through a sequence of dependent sampling steps. Because later steps depend on earlier ones, this process can take substantial time even after the model has been trained. This paper asks how to reorganize those dependencies so that more of the sampling work can happen in parallel.

The authors express sampling as a system of triangular nonlinear equations and solve it through fixed-point iteration. This formulation gives them a systematic way to develop techniques that reduce the number of solver iterations. Their resulting algorithm, ParaTAA, requires no model training and uses additional computation and memory to accelerate sampling.

Experiments report a four- to fourteen-fold reduction in inference steps relative to common sequential samplers, including DDIM and DDPM. In the highlighted Stable Diffusion example, ParaTAA reproduces the images from a 100-step DDIM run using seven inference steps. These results concern fewer sequential inference steps; the approach explicitly trades extra computational and memory resources for faster generation.
icml-2024-accelerating-parallel-sampling.tldr: ParaTAA reformulates diffusion sampling as a parallel equation-solving problem, reducing inference steps without retraining while using extra computation and memory.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to learn across tasks while maintaining its performance. Some methods address this by changing the network architecture, adding new branches to increase its width. This paper argues that such methods leave out another important architectural choice: depth. Its goal is to adapt both dimensions as part of the learning process.

The proposed method uses a non-parametric Bayesian approach to infer network depth and adapt width. Specifically, a beta process models growth in depth, while a conjugate Bernoulli process applies drop-connect regularization to width. These components place depth growth and connection-level regularization within a shared probabilistic framework, rather than treating architectural adaptation solely as the addition of branches.

Across continual-learning benchmarks, the method achieves performance that is superior to or comparable with state-of-the-art alternatives. The authors also extend it to unsupervised continual learning and report competitive results. The contribution therefore combines a broader treatment of architectural adaptation with empirical evidence that it can work across both supervised and unsupervised continual-learning settings.
icml-2024-bayesian-adaptation-of-network.tldr: A Bayesian approach jointly adapts network depth and width, achieving competitive or superior performance across continual-learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning must accommodate differences between clients while avoiding misleading correlations that fail when data distributions change. This creates a difficult distinction: useful personalized features and unreliable shortcuts can both vary across clients. Removing everything that varies could therefore discard the very information needed for personalization.

The authors analyze client data generation through a structured causal model. They propose a causal signature that uses globally invariant features as an anchor to distinguish personalized information from spurious information. They then express this signature as an information-theoretic constraint, which guides each client toward personalized representations that avoid shortcuts. The resulting method is called FedPIN.

The theoretical analysis shows that FedPIN can obtain a tighter generalization-error bound than prevalent personalized federated approaches when clients experience a training-to-test distribution shift. The paper also provides a convergence-rate guarantee. Experiments report stronger out-of-distribution generalization than state-of-the-art competitors, supporting the value of separating useful client-specific information from correlations that merely happen to hold during training.
icml-2024-causally-motivated-personalize.tldr: FedPIN uses a causal, information-theoretic constraint to preserve client personalization while reducing shortcuts that undermine generalization under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Support vector machines and quantile regression become computationally challenging with high-dimensional data partly because their loss functions are not smooth. This lack of smoothness limits the use of efficient coordinate-descent techniques. The paper introduces the finite smoothing algorithm, or FSA, to make those optimization problems easier to compute.

FSA replaces the non-smooth losses with smooth counterparts so that efficient computation becomes possible. The key theoretical point is that smoothing does not necessarily restrict the method to an approximate answer: the authors show that FSA can yield exact solutions. This matters because improving the convenience of optimization would be less useful if it necessarily changed the solution being sought.

In simulations and benchmark tests, FSA runs substantially faster than competing methods, often by orders of magnitude, while maintaining or improving precision. The authors implement the approach in two open-source R packages, hdsvm and hdqr. Together, the theory and evaluations support smoothing as a practical route to faster high-dimensional optimization without an unavoidable loss of solution accuracy.
icml-2024-finite-smoothing-algorithm-for.tldr: FSA smooths difficult loss functions to accelerate high-dimensional SVM and quantile-regression optimization while retaining the ability to obtain exact solutions.

paragraphs: Learning robot control from diverse trajectories requires a model to understand how movement changes over time. Transformers can model these changing features, but the paper identifies data efficiency and inference latency as obstacles. The authors start from an observation about robot trajectories: much of their frequency-domain energy lies in the low-frequency components.

Their Fourier Controller Network, FCNet, builds on that observation by representing temporal features in the frequency domain. It uses the Short-Time Fourier Transform to extract those features and frequency-domain interpolation to encode them. The architecture also incorporates the Fast Fourier Transform and Sliding Discrete Fourier Transform, supporting parallel training alongside efficient recurrent inference for real-time decisions.

Experiments in simulated environments and real-world robot locomotion report strong efficiency and effectiveness relative to existing methods. FCNet outperforms a Transformer on the evaluated multi-environment robotics datasets across sizes from 1.9 million to 120 million. The findings support frequency-based temporal modeling as a useful control architecture across the tested data scales and environments.
icml-2024-fourier-controller-networks-fo.tldr: FCNet models robot trajectories in the frequency domain to support efficient training and real-time control, outperforming Transformers across the evaluated dataset sizes.

paragraphs: Offline preference optimization fine-tunes large models using an existing collection of preference data. This paper introduces generalized preference optimization, or GPO, as a common framework for several methods used in this process. The aim is to explain how these methods relate and provide a way to develop additional variants.

GPO defines a family of training losses through a general class of convex functions. A loss specifies what training should penalize; choosing its defining function produces different members of the family. Existing algorithms, including DPO, IPO, and SLiC, appear as special cases. This makes their relationship explicit within a shared mathematical framework.

The choice of function also helps explain how each method imposes regularization, which constrains the changes encouraged by preference training. The authors use analysis and experiments to examine how this offline regularization relates to the KL-divergence regularization intended in the canonical reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback formulation. They identify both connections and subtle differences between the two.

In a controlled setting, different GPO variants achieve similar trade-offs between regularization and performance. However, their best hyperparameter values can differ, consistent with the theory. The finding suggests that choosing a variant and tuning it are connected decisions: similar trade-offs do not imply that the same settings work best across methods.
icml-2024-generalized-preference-optimiz.tldr: GPO unifies several offline preference-training methods and explains how their loss functions shape regularization, with variants achieving similar performance trade-offs in a controlled setting.

paragraphs: This paper examines what several self-supervised learning objectives encourage representations to retain. It begins with two methods that use paired branches, Barlow Twins and spectral contrastive learning, and analyzes them using matrix-based measures of information. The authors prove that both losses implicitly optimize matrix mutual information and matrix joint entropy.

The analysis then moves to single-branch masked autoencoders, specifically MAE and U-MAE. In this setting, the information quantities reduce to entropy. This connection motivates the Matrix Variational Masked Auto-Encoder, M-MAE, which adds a matrix-based entropy estimate as a regularizer. The formulation also includes U-MAE as a special case, linking the new method to an existing approach.

Empirical evaluations report improvements over state-of-the-art methods on ImageNet, including a 3.9% improvement in linear probing with ViT-Base and a 1% improvement in fine-tuning with ViT-Large. The contribution connects an explanation of existing objectives with a new training method: the information-based analysis supplies a concrete regularizer whose usefulness is then tested experimentally.
icml-2024-information-flow-in-self-super.tldr: A matrix-information analysis of self-supervised objectives motivates M-MAE, an entropy-regularized masked autoencoder with reported ImageNet improvements.

paragraphs: Asymmetric kernel singular value decomposition extends kernel learning beyond the symmetric kernels used in methods such as kernel principal component analysis. However, the existing formulation has significant mathematical obstacles: it cannot accommodate infinite-dimensional feature mappings, and its variational objective can be unbounded. This paper develops a new formulation and investigates its practical usefulness.

The authors construct a coupled covariance eigenproblem using covariance operators. This permits infinite-dimensional feature maps, while the solution can ultimately be obtained through the singular value decomposition of an induced asymmetric kernel matrix. They also derive an asymmetric Nyström method from paired adjoint eigenfunction equations, using a finite-sample approximation to accelerate training.

The paper provides empirical evaluations across multiple tasks, comparing asymmetric kernel SVD with approaches that symmetrize the problem or use linear SVD. These experiments support the practical utility of the asymmetric approach. The overall contribution connects a more accommodating mathematical formulation, a training approximation, and empirical evidence for learning directly with asymmetric kernel structure.
icml-2024-learning-in-feature-spaces-via.tldr: A coupled-covariance formulation enables asymmetric kernel learning with infinite-dimensional feature maps and introduces a Nyström approximation to speed training.

paragraphs: The quadratic assignment problem is a difficult combinatorial optimization problem involving facilities and locations. The paper emphasizes its strong computational hardness: a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme would imply P equals NP. Against that background, the authors focus on learned methods that improve existing solutions, addressing the limited scale and computational inefficiency of prior approaches.

Their design encodes facility nodes and location nodes separately, avoiding the computationally intensive association graphs used in existing methods. This representation supports larger problem sizes. The Solution AWare Transformer, or SAWT, then incorporates the current solution matrix into its attention scores, allowing its representation of the problem to depend explicitly on the assignment being improved.

This solution-aware attention is intended to capture higher-order information relevant to quadratic assignment. Experiments on generated instances of different sizes and the QAPLIB benchmark validate the model’s effectiveness. The contribution is a scalable learned improvement approach supported by experiments; the computational-hardness discussion explains why efficient solution methods remain valuable without suggesting that the underlying complexity barrier has disappeared.
icml-2024-learning-solution-aware-transf.tldr: SAWT improves quadratic-assignment solutions using separate facility and location encodings and attention conditioned on the current assignment.

paragraphs: MathScale addresses mathematical reasoning by improving the data used to instruction-tune language models. It uses a frontier language model to extract topics and knowledge points from seed questions, then organizes them into a concept graph. That graph guides the generation of new mathematical questions, giving data expansion an explicit conceptual structure.

Using this process, the authors create MathScaleQA, a dataset containing two million question-answer pairs. They also assemble MWPBench to evaluate mathematical word-problem solving across nine datasets, including GSM8K and MATH. Its coverage spans school, college, and competition mathematics, allowing the resulting models to be evaluated across different levels of mathematical difficulty.

Fine-tuning open-source models such as LLaMA-2 and Mistral on MathScaleQA substantially improves their mathematical reasoning in the reported evaluations. MathScale-7B achieves state-of-the-art performance across MWPBench datasets, exceeding its best similarly sized peers by 42.8% in micro-average accuracy and 43.6% in macro-average accuracy. The findings support concept-guided data generation as an effective way to scale mathematical instruction tuning.
icml-2024-mathscale-scaling-instruction-.tldr: MathScale uses a concept graph to generate mathematical training data at scale, producing substantial benchmark gains for fine-tuned language models.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a trained diffusion model reveals that a particular example appeared in its training data. That question defines a membership-inference attack. The authors use reconstruction loss as evidence, but their approach accounts for the fact that the appropriate comparison threshold can differ from one example to another.

They train quantile-regression models to predict a quantile of reconstruction losses for examples excluded from training. These predictions provide example-specific thresholds for a hypothesis test of membership. The paper also introduces a bootstrap procedure that combines a collection of weaker attackers through majority voting, improving accuracy over individual quantile-regression models.

The proposed attack outperforms the previous state-of-the-art attack while requiring substantially less computation. Earlier attacks trained multiple shadow models with the same architecture as the target model; this approach trains much smaller models instead. The findings demonstrate a privacy vulnerability and show that tailored statistical thresholds can make membership testing both more accurate and less computationally demanding in the evaluated setting.
icml-2024-membership-inference-attacks-o.tldr: Example-specific reconstruction-loss thresholds enable a more accurate, less computationally expensive membership-inference attack on diffusion models.

paragraphs: Combining task-specific vision Transformers into a single model offers a way to support multiple tasks together. A central problem is parameter interference: weights that work well for one task can conflict with weights learned for another. Existing merging methods commonly seek one static combination within the original parameter space.

The authors instead merge most parameters while expanding the Transformer layers’ MLP components into weight-ensembling mixture-of-experts modules. These modules combine shared and task-specific knowledge dynamically according to the input. The central idea is to separate those two kinds of knowledge before recombining them, giving each instance a more flexible mixture than a fixed merged model can provide.

The paper evaluates the method through conventional multi-task model-merging experiments and assessments of generalization and robustness. The reported results support its effectiveness in mitigating interference. Its architectural contribution concentrates adaptability in the MLP components while retaining a largely merged model, showing how input-dependent weight combinations can help reconcile knowledge learned by different task-specific models.
icml-2024-merging-multi-task-models-via-.tldr: Weight-ensembling expert modules dynamically combine shared and task-specific knowledge to reduce interference when merging vision Transformers.

paragraphs: Monotonic linear interpolation describes an observation about model parameters: error can decrease steadily along the straight line from initialization to a trained solution. Earlier explanations connected this behavior to the smoothness of the optimization trajectory. This paper tests whether the original initialization is actually central to the observed pattern.

The authors find that error curves can still decrease monotonically when the initial parameters are replaced by noise or even zeros. This suggests that the pattern may depend primarily on properties of the converged model. They investigate how a scaled version of that model relates to the original and introduce generalized, rectified, and normalized forms of scale invariance for different cases.

Their interpretation rewrites interpolation as a nearly scale-invariant trained network plus a noise term whose magnitude changes. Viewed in reverse, increasing the noise raises error monotonically. Interpolation from the actual initialization becomes a special case in which that initialization supplies the noise term. This reframing shifts attention toward the endpoint’s properties without establishing that optimization trajectories are universally irrelevant.
icml-2024-mli-formula-a-nearly-scale-inv.tldr: The paper interprets monotonic interpolation through near scale invariance and changing noise, suggesting trained-model properties may explain much of the phenomenon.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines a small amount of labeled data with a larger pool of unlabeled examples. Many approaches use self-training to generate class targets and then encourage predictions to match them. The paper identifies a weakness in that emphasis: matching predictions to individual classes can overlook meaningful relationships among the classes themselves.

OTMatch incorporates those semantic relationships through an optimal-transport loss for matching distributions. This makes relationships between classes part of the learning objective, rather than relying only on alignment with a generated class target. The proposed change therefore concerns how information from unlabeled examples guides training and how class structure enters that guidance.

The authors evaluate OTMatch on standard vision and language datasets and report improvements over baseline methods. Those results support the usefulness of semantic class relationships in the tested semi-supervised settings. The broader significance is that unlabeled-data learning can benefit from a richer notion of agreement between distributions, one that incorporates relationships among possible outcomes alongside the predictions assigned to individual examples.
icml-2024-otmatch-improving-semi-supervi.tldr: OTMatch uses optimal transport to incorporate semantic relationships among classes, improving semi-supervised learning on evaluated vision and language datasets.

paragraphs: Generating convincing data and reliably measuring how realistic data is are closely connected problems, but progress on one does not automatically solve the other. This position paper examines the measurement problem: how to design a function that distinguishes realistic examples from unrealistic ones. It argues that this remains difficult and poorly understood despite advances in generation.

The authors use ideas from algorithmic information theory to discuss why realism is challenging to quantify and why a good generative model alone is insufficient. They introduce the concept of a universal critic as a description of what a suitable solution could look like. Unlike adversarial critics, this proposed critic does not require adversarial training.

The authors explicitly present universal critics as not immediately practical. Their value is conceptual: they provide a target for practical designs and a means of analyzing existing attempts to measure realism. The paper’s contribution is therefore a framework for reasoning about realism assessment, including why strong generation capability does not by itself supply a reliable realism score.
icml-2024-position-what-makes-an-image-r.tldr: This position paper introduces universal critics as a theoretical guide to measuring realism, a problem that good generative models alone do not solve.

paragraphs: An explanation that highlights an image region can show where a classifier focuses without identifying what visual feature it recognizes there. Part-prototype networks address both questions by representing recognizable parts, such as characteristic wings or heads. However, existing versions often sacrifice accuracy compared with their black-box counterparts.

This paper constructs part-prototype explanations after a model has already been trained. It decomposes the classification head into interpretable prototypes using an unsupervised discovery and refinement strategy. The crucial requirement is that the prototypes precisely reconstruct the original classification head. That reconstruction is how the method preserves the trained model’s performance while providing an interpretable representation of its classification mechanism.

The authors report more faithful explanations in qualitative comparisons and better part-prototypes in quantitative comparisons with prior part-prototype networks. The contribution brings together two properties that had been difficult to combine: explanations of both feature identity and location, and preservation of the original classifier’s performance through a post-hoc decomposition.
icml-2024-post-hoc-part-prototype-networ.tldr: A post-hoc decomposition reconstructs a trained classifier’s head with interpretable part-prototypes, preserving performance while explaining what features matter and where.

paragraphs: This paper proposes positional encodings for graph neural networks derived from quantum systems. The approach maps a graph’s topology onto interactions between qubits, then uses the resulting quantum correlations to construct features. Its motivation is that long-range correlations in these systems may provide useful structural information for models processing graphs.

The authors prove that some of the proposed quantum features are more expressive than commonly used relative random-walk probabilities for certain graphs. That qualification matters: the result establishes an advantage for particular features and graph cases, rather than a universal ordering of all quantum and classical encodings. It gives a theoretical reason to investigate these representations.

Experiments use tractable versions of the quantum features and show improvements to state-of-the-art models on standard benchmarks and large-scale datasets. The combination of theory and empirical results supports their potential for improving graph learning, including graph Transformers. The practical evidence concerns the computed tractable features, while the broader proposal explores how quantum-computing capabilities could enrich graph representations.
icml-2024-quantum-positional-encodings-f.tldr: Quantum-derived graph encodings offer greater expressiveness in certain cases, and tractable versions improve evaluated graph-learning models.

paragraphs: Image restoration should improve an image while preserving its original structures, but learned restoration methods can struggle with that requirement. This paper formulates restoration as an optimal-transport problem in both paired and unpaired settings. Its central idea is to use the transport residual as information about the particular degradation affecting an image.

Residual-Conditioned Optimal Transport, or RCOT, uses this information in two places. A Fourier residual-guided objective incorporates it into the transport cost. A two-pass restoration map also uses it to guide prediction: a base model first produces a residual, which is encoded into a degradation-specific embedding that conditions a second refinement pass.

Using duality, the authors convert the formulation into a minimax problem that can be optimized by adversarially training neural networks. Experiments across multiple restoration tasks show competitive distortion measures and perceptual quality, with more faithful structures than state-of-the-art methods. The results support using an initial restoration’s residual as an explicit cue for both the objective and subsequent refinement.
icml-2024-residual-conditioned-optimal-t.tldr: RCOT uses restoration residuals to guide an optimal-transport objective and a second refinement pass, improving structural fidelity in evaluated restoration tasks.

paragraphs: Language models intended for mobile devices face tight computation and memory constraints. This paper investigates how to improve small models by examining training and architectural choices that can receive limited attention in a complex training pipeline. The authors organize their empirical study around a model with one billion parameters.

They examine three areas: neural architecture, parameter initialization, and optimization strategy. The resulting design recommendations include tokenizer compression, architectural changes, parameter inheritance, and multiple-round training. Following these findings, they train PanGu-π-1B Pro and PanGu-π-1.5B Pro on a multilingual corpus reported at a scale of 1.6 trillion.

The improved optimization and architecture produce a reported average benchmark improvement of 8.87 for PanGu-π-1B Pro. The 1.5-billion-parameter version also surpasses a range of state-of-the-art models with larger parameter counts. These empirical results show that carefully chosen training and design details can materially improve small-model performance, and that model size alone does not determine the relative performance observed in these evaluations.
icml-2024-rethinking-optimization-and-ar.tldr: An empirical study of architecture, initialization, and optimization yields training recipes that substantially improve small PanGu language models.

paragraphs: Mixup augments training data by combining pairs of examples. Selective mixup chooses particular pairs, such as examples from different classes or domains, and has performed well under distribution shifts. This paper examines an overlooked consequence of that selection: choosing pairs non-randomly also changes the distribution of examples used during training.

The authors show that this resampling effect can improve generalization independently of the mixing operation. In binary classification, for instance, selecting pairs across classes implicitly produces a uniform class distribution, connecting the method to a classical response to label shift. Experiments verify that resampling accounts for some improvements previously attributed to selective mixup.

The theoretical account depends on a regression-toward-the-mean property that the authors find in several datasets and describe as accidental. Their analysis predicts a previously unrecognized failure mode and conditions under which selective mixup can hurt performance. It also motivates improved variants that deliberately combine mixing and resampling, making pair selection an explicit part of the method’s explanation and design.
icml-2024-selective-mixup-helps-with-dis.tldr: Selective mixup gains partly arise from implicit resampling, an insight that explains some successes, predicts failures, and guides improved variants.

paragraphs: Sleep recordings contain complementary information from brain activity, cardiac signals, and respiration. The authors curate more than 100,000 hours of these recordings from over 14,000 participants and use them to develop SleepFM, a multimodal foundation model for sleep analysis. The objective is to learn representations that bring these different physiological measurements together.

A central methodological contribution is a leave-one-out contrastive-learning approach. The authors show that its representations improve downstream performance compared with standard pairwise contrastive learning. They assess the learned embeddings using logistic regression, allowing the evaluation to test how useful those representations are for sleep-stage classification and sleep-disordered breathing detection.

Logistic regression on SleepFM embeddings outperforms an end-to-end CNN on both tasks. For sleep-stage classification, macro AUROC is 0.88 versus 0.72; for breathing detection, AUROC is 0.85 versus 0.69. The embeddings also achieve 48% top-1 average accuracy when retrieving modality clip pairs from 90,000 candidates. Together, these findings support learning relationships across sleep-recording modalities as a useful source of task-relevant representations.
icml-2024-sleepfm-multi-modal-representa.tldr: SleepFM learns joint representations of brain, cardiac, and respiratory recordings that improve evaluated sleep-analysis tasks and cross-modality retrieval.

paragraphs: Sparse training commonly aims to reduce computation by removing weights, but the resulting accuracy loss can require longer training. Sparse-IFT investigates a different use of sparsity: improving accuracy while keeping the floating-point operation budget of a dense model. This makes accuracy at a fixed computational budget the central objective.

The proposed transformations replace dense layers using a single sparsity-level hyperparameter and expand the space of possible sparse masks. Dynamic sparse training then explores this larger space of masks and weights. A spectral analysis using Ramanujan graph properties supports the approach, and the study identifies a strong correlation among mask topology, learned weights, and final performance.

Without changing training hyperparameters, the authors report improvements including 3.5% for ResNet-18 on ImageNet and 0.9% for GPT-3 Small on the Open LLM leaderboard. These findings support sparse transformations as a means of improving models under a fixed FLOP budget. They also emphasize that the pattern of retained connections matters alongside the numerical values of their weights.
icml-2024-sparse-ift-sparse-iso-flop-tra.tldr: Sparse-IFT uses sparsity to expand architectural choices and improve accuracy while maintaining the computation budget of dense models.

paragraphs: Quantum-state classification uses statistics from quantum measurements to distinguish states with different properties. Supervised methods require labeled measurement outcomes, but obtaining those labels can demand computation and memory that grow exponentially with the number of qubits. SSL4Q addresses this bottleneck through semi-supervised learning designed specifically for quantum-state classification.

Its architecture accounts for two characteristics of the data. Quantum measurements are unordered, so the model is designed to be invariant to their permutation. Measurements also contain uncertainty, and the architecture is designed to remain robust to it. These choices adapt the learning method to the structure of quantum measurement data while reducing reliance on extensive labels.

The authors evaluate SSL4Q in simulations involving the Heisenberg model and variational quantum circuit model, with systems reaching 50 qubits. In settings with limited labels, the numerical results outperform traditional supervised models. The evidence supports the potential of semi-supervised learning to classify quantum states with reduced labeling-related resource demands in the studied systems.
icml-2024-ssl4q-semi-supervised-learning.tldr: SSL4Q adapts semi-supervised learning to unordered, uncertain quantum measurements and outperforms supervised models in evaluated settings with limited labels.

paragraphs: Using language models for visual synthesis requires a representation of visual information as tokens. Traditional approaches turn raster images into discrete grid tokens through specialized visual modules. This paper argues that the grid representation disrupts the capture of meaningful visual structure and proposes vector graphics as a more semantically coherent alternative.

StrokeNUWA represents vector graphics with stroke tokens. The authors describe these tokens as rich in visual semantics, compatible with language models, and highly compressed. The representation is central to the proposal: choosing strokes as the units of generation is intended to preserve meaningful visual groupings while providing a compact sequence for the model to process.

On vector-graphic generation tasks, StrokeNUWA substantially surpasses traditional language-model-based and optimization-based methods across the evaluated metrics. The authors report inference speedups of up to 94 times and an SVG code compression ratio of 6.9%. These results support the value of changing the visual token representation, with the maximum reported speedup applying to the comparisons made in the paper.
icml-2024-strokenuwatokenizing-strokes-f.tldr: StrokeNUWA uses compact stroke tokens for vector-graphic synthesis, improving evaluated generation metrics and achieving inference speedups of up to 94 times.
